content.text:
Base directory for this skill: c:\Users\rober\Documents\Projects\Nuuly_Inventory_Assessment\.claude\skills\feature

# /feature: One big testing feature (oversell hardening + contract): (a) negative-control test proving the race tests catch a naive read-then-write purchase, (b) multi-instance purchase race (two app instances, one Postgres), (c) HTTP load test with final quantities checked, (d) property-based test against an in-memory model, (e) contract-validation test of responses vs inventory.yaml; optionally raise @RepeatedTest counts / stress profile. Then fix README claims to match. Plan-step decisions to put to Robert: order, each new dependency/tool, how naive code stays out of src/main, whether load test runs in ./gradlew test, whether he writes any tests himself.

Follow these steps in order. Do not skip one because the feature looks small.

**Robert writes the production code; you coach.** Never create or edit files under `src/main/`
unless Robert explicitly asks for that specific edit (see "Who writes what" in `CLAUDE.md`).
Your deliverables are the contract check, the plan, the tests, hints, reviews and the docs.

## 0. Gate: previous walkthrough done?

Check the newest file in `docs/learning/walkthroughs/`. If there are commits touching
`src/` after the commit it records, a walkthrough is still owed. Tell Robert and suggest
running `/walkthrough` first. Continue only if he says to.

## 1. Pin the behavior to the contract

Read `src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml` and quote the exact part this feature implements.
List the acceptance criteria as a checklist: method + path, request schema and validation,
every response status with its content type (`application/json` vs `text/plain`), and body shape.
List any ambiguity the contract leaves open and ask Robert how to resolve it.

## 2. Plan, then wait for approval

Give a short plan covering:

- the files Robert will create or change, each one's layer (controller / service / repository /
  model / migration), and what each needs to do, described in words and signatures, not code;
- the test files you will write, and which acceptance criterion each test covers;
- the Kotlin and Spring concepts this feature introduces for the first time. That list is both
  what you'll coach him through and the agenda for the walkthrough.

**Stop and wait for Robert to approve the plan.**

## 3. Write the failing tests

- Write the tests under `src/test/` first: at least one per acceptance criterion, covering the
  error paths as well as the happy path. They are the spec for Robert's code.
- Tests reference the classes and functions named in the plan. The build won't compile until he
  creates them; that's expected. Tell him which compile errors and failures to expect.
- Follow the documentation standard in `CLAUDE.md` for the test files (KDoc, `// Why:`, notes
  header line).

## 4. Robert writes the code; you coach

- Create the marker file `.claude/coding-in-progress` (gitignored). While it exists, the
  `check_notes` Stop hook skips `src/main/`, so it won't push you to document half-finished code.
- Hand over a short checklist: which file to write next and what it must do, in request-path
  order (usually migration → model → repository → service → controller). Suggest a first
  test to make pass.
- **Hints go in increasing order**: the concept → the API or annotation to look up → the shape
  of the code in words → a code snippet, but only when he asks, and in chat for him to type.
  Never write the file for him.
- Explain concepts when he asks or when you see him stuck on one, with the Java equivalent
  when that helps.
- Run the build (`.\gradlew.bat build` in PowerShell) when he asks, and explain failures in terms of what his
  code does. Report results truthfully.
- The KDoc hook only runs on your edits, so remind him that every non-private declaration he
  writes needs KDoc, plus the `// Study notes:` header line.
- While his code is in progress, its study notes are expected to lag. Don't write notes for
  half-finished code.
- If you ever try to edit `src/main/`, the `code_guard` hook asks Robert for approval. Don't
  request that unless he asked for that specific edit.

## 4b. Review

When the tests pass, review his code: contract conformance, idiomatic Kotlin (flag
Java-style Kotlin and explain the idiom), the documentation standard, and anything the tests
don't catch. Explain each point; he makes the changes. Rerun the build after his fixes.

## 5. Documentation

Once the build is green and the review is done, run `/sync-docs`. It writes or updates the
study notes for every changed file (describing the code Robert wrote), the concepts
index, the README (endpoint status, curl examples, decision records) and the TODO, then runs
the `doc-reviewer` agent until it returns `PASS`. Tell Robert what the reviewer caught.

## 6. Check the docs gate

`python scripts/check_notes.py` must print nothing. (The Stop hook enforces this too.)

## 7. Hand-off

Summarize what Robert built and what he learned along the way. Propose a commit message (small and descriptive, ending with the
attribution line from the system reminder), and commit only if Robert says so. Finish with:
"Ready for `/walkthrough`, then `/ship`." Do not start another feature in this turn.

## Oversell protection: test plan

**Invariant: a purchase must never oversell, even when requests arrive at the same moment.**
Stock never goes below zero, and every unit sold was actually in stock. Test this at every
level we build, using several different mechanisms, because each one catches a different
class of bug. Each item below is also a teaching topic for a walkthrough.

### Correctness in isolation
- [x] Repository tests against a real Postgres (Testcontainers, not H2): purchase exact stock → 0,
      purchase stock + 1 → rejected and quantity unchanged, purchase on missing SKU → not found
      (`removeStock` tests, green 2026-09-29)
- [x] Controller tests (`MockMvc`): 400 with `text/plain` body on insufficient stock, 404 on missing SKU (green 2026-09-29)

### Concurrency
- [x] **Same-SKU purchase race.** Seed stock S, fire N > S concurrent purchases of 1 through
      a start gate (`CountDownLatch` or coroutines) so they really overlap. Assert: exactly S
      succeed (200), N − S are rejected (400), final quantity is 0, never negative.
      (`InventoryConcurrencyTest`, at the repository level; green 2026-09-29)
- [x] **Uneven quantities.** Concurrent purchases of different sizes. Assert: the sum of
      successful purchases ≤ S, and final = S − sum(successful). (green 2026-09-29)
- [x] **Mixed receive + purchase race.** Concurrent restocks and purchases. Assert:
      final = initial + sum(received) − sum(successful purchases). (green 2026-09-29)
- [x] **New-SKU creation race.** Concurrent first-time `POST`s for a SKU that doesn't exist yet.
      All succeed, no duplicate-key errors, final = sum of all quantities.
      (`InventoryConcurrencyTest`, plus a lost-update race on an existing SKU; green with `addStock`, 2026-09-28)
- [ ] **Repeat to flush out flakiness.** Run the race tests many times (`@RepeatedTest`), since
      concurrency bugs are intermittent. (all five races use `@RepeatedTest(5)`, 2026-09-29; raise the count
      or add a stress profile if "many times" should mean more)
- [ ] **Negative control.** Temporarily swap in a naive read-then-write implementation and show
      the race test *fails*. This proves the test can actually detect an oversell.

### Database backstop
- [x] Test that the `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint rejects a direct update that would go
      negative, so the database protects the data even if the application has a bug.
      (`database rejects an update that would make quantity negative` in `InventoryRepositoryTest`; green since V1)

### Across instances and under load
- [ ] **Multiple app instances.** Two app instances (or two Spring contexts) against the same
      Postgres, running the purchase race. Correctness must hold because the database enforces it.
- [ ] **HTTP load test.** Gatling (it has a Kotlin DSL) or k6 against the running app: sustained
      concurrent purchases on hot SKUs, then check the final quantities with `GET /inventory`.

### Model-based (stretch)
- [ ] Property-based test (e.g. Kotest property testing): random sequences of receive and
      purchase operations checked against a simple in-memory model. The invariant must hold
      after every sequence.

openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Inventory API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /inventory/{skuId}:
    parameters:
      - name: skuId
        in: path
        required: true
        schema:
          type: string
          example: CW-XYCS-BM-01
    get:
      summary: Get inventory for a SKU
      description: Returns the current quantity on hand for the specified SKU. Returns 404 if the SKU does not exist.
      operationId: getInventory
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Current inventory state for the sku
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryItem'
        '404':
          description: SKU not found
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
    post:
      summary: Create or update inventory for a SKU
      description: >
        Adds stock for the specified SKU. If the SKU does not yet exist in inventory,
        it is created with the given quantity. If it already exists, the quantity is
        added to the current stock. Returns the updated inventory state for the SKU.
      operationId: createInventory
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryQuantity'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Current state of the item after update
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryItem'
        '400':
          description: Invalid request
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
  /inventory/{skuId}/purchase:
    parameters:
      - name: skuId
        in: path
        required: true
        schema:
          type: string
          example: widget
    post:
      summary: Purchase a quantity of a SKU
      description: >
        Deducts the requested quantity from inventory for the specified SKU.
        The purchase is only allowed if the current stock is sufficient to
        fulfill the full requested quantity. Returns 404 if the SKU does not
        exist. Returns 400 if there is insufficient inventory. On success, returns the
        remaining inventory for the SKU.
      operationId: purchaseItem
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryQuantity'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Purchase successful; remaining inventory for the item
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryItem'
        '400':
          description: Insufficient inventory or invalid request
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
        '404':
          description: SKU not found
          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
  /inventory:
    get:
      summary: List all inventory
      description: >
        Returns a list of all SKUs currently in inventory along with their quantities.
        If no SKUs exist, returns an empty array.
      operationId: listInventory
      responses:
        '200':
          description: List of all inventory items
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/InventoryItem'  
components:
  schemas:
    InventoryQuantity:
      type: object
      required:
        - quantity
      properties:
        quantity:
          type: integer
          minimum: 1
          example: 10
    InventoryItem:
      type: object
      properties:
        skuId:
          type: string
          example: widget
        quantity:
          type: integer
          minimum: 0
          example: 10
    Error:
      type: string
      example: Insufficient inventory
- **In-memory map:** needs no setup, but data is lost on restart and it only works with a
  single instance.
- **H2:** its SQL dialect differs from production databases.
- **Redis / document stores:** add nothing for a single integer per key.

Kotlin doesn't favor any particular database; it uses the same JDBC drivers as Java. It does
favor data-access libraries that work with immutable `data class`es (`JdbcClient`, Spring Data
JDBC, Exposed) over JPA, which needs compiler plugins to work around Kotlin's final-by-default classes.

The oversell guarantee is tested with several different mechanisms: race tests, a negative
control, multi-instance tests, load tests and property-based tests. The full plan is in
[.claude/TODO.md](.claude/TODO.md#oversell-protection-test-plan).

**Prerequisites:** JDK 21 and Docker Desktop (running). Postgres starts automatically in a
container; there is nothing to install or configure by hand.

```sh
./gradlew bootRun   # start the API on http://localhost:8080 (Windows PowerShell: .\gradlew.bat bootRun)

The walkthrough gate passes. The only `src/` commits after the purchase walkthrough are the comment rewordings it already covered. I've also created the branch `test/oversell-hardening` from an up-to-date `main`.

## 1. Contract check

This feature adds tests, not endpoints, so there's no new behavior to pin down. The contract-validation test does check all four operations in `inventory.yaml`:

- [ ] `GET /inventory` returns 200 `application/json` with an array of `InventoryItem`
- [ ] `GET /inventory/{skuId}` returns 200 `application/json` `InventoryItem`, or 404 `text/plain` `Error` (a string)
- [ ] `POST /inventory/{skuId}` returns 200 `application/json` `InventoryItem`, or 400 `text/plain`
- [ ] `POST /inventory/{skuId}/purchase` returns 200 `application/json` `InventoryItem`, or 400 or 404 `text/plain`
- [ ] Requests use the `InventoryQuantity` schema (`quantity` is a required integer, `minimum: 1`). `InventoryItem.quantity` has `minimum: 0`.

**Ambiguity:** `InventoryItem` marks no properties as `required` and doesn't forbid extra fields. A plain schema validator would accept `{}`. I suggest the test also asserts that both fields are present and that nothing extra comes back. That's stricter than the YAML, but it matches what the endpoints actually promise.

## 2. Plan

Almost everything here is test code, so the `src/main/` rule doesn't really come into play. Every piece lands as its own small commit.

| # | Part | Test files | How it works |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Shared helper | `support/Race.kt` | Move `race()` out of `InventoryConcurrencyTest` so every part below can use it. |
| a | Negative control | `NaiveInventoryRepository.kt` + `NegativeControlTest.kt` | A naive purchase in `src/test`: read, check in Kotlin, then write the absolute value. It runs through the same race, and the test asserts that the same invariant check **catches** the oversell. A `CyclicBarrier` between the read and the write makes the lost update happen on every run instead of only sometimes. |
| e | Contract validation | `InventoryContractTest.kt` | Checks every status code of every operation against `inventory.yaml` through MockMvc. |
| d | Property-based | `InventoryModelPropertyTest.kt` | Random sequences of receive and purchase calls on a few SKUs run against the real repository and a simple in-memory model at the same time. After every step, the result and the stored quantity must match the model. |
| b | Multi-instance | `MultiInstanceRaceTest.kt` | Two full Spring apps start on random ports against the same Testcontainers Postgres. Buyers are split across both apps, and the invariants must hold. |
| c | HTTP load | `InventoryLoadTest.kt` + a Gradle `loadTest` task | Sustained concurrent purchases on a few popular SKUs, then check the final quantities with `GET /inventory`. |
| — | Docs | README, TODO | Make the README's testing claims match what exists (gap audit items 2 and 3). |

**New concepts** (also the walkthrough agenda):
- a `CyclicBarrier` to force a specific interleaving of threads
- sharing test helpers as top-level functions
- OpenAPI response validation
- Kotest `Arb` generators and `checkAll`, with your first contact with coroutines (`suspend`, `runBlocking`)
- model-based testing
- `SpringApplicationBuilder` to run two app contexts
- `java.net.http.HttpClient` and virtual threads
- JUnit `@Tag` and a custom Gradle `Test` task

**My recommendations for the rest:**
- **Order:** 0 → a → e → d → b → c → docs. It goes from no new dependencies to the heaviest setup.
- **`@RepeatedTest`:** keep it at 5 in the normal build and let the `loadTest` task provide the volume.

// Study notes: docs/learning/notes/main/inventory/PurchaseResult.kt.md

package com.robertwoolbright.inventory.inventory

// Why: We used the sealed interface because we have 3 possible outcomes we need to account for. Not just a success or null so returning InventoryItem? doesn't help us between when we need to throw 404 or 400.

/** PurchaseResult is returned by the repository and translated by the service. */
sealed interface PurchaseResult {
    
    /** The SKU exists and had enough stock. Item holds the remaining stock. */
    data class Purchased(val item: InventoryItem) : PurchaseResult
    
    /** There's no row for that SKU id. */
    data object SkuNotFound : PurchaseResult
    
    /** The row exists but has less than the requested quantity. */
    data object InsufficientStock : PurchaseResult
    
}// Study notes: docs/learning/notes/main/inventory/InventoryItem.kt.md

55	### The start gate
56	
57	```kotlin
58	// Why: a start gate. Every thread first checks in on `ready`, then waits on `start`; releasing
59	// `start` once makes them all hit the database together instead of one after another.
60	private fun <T> race(threads: Int, action: (Int) -> T): List<Result<T>> {
61	    val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)
62	    val ready = CountDownLatch(threads)
63	    val start = CountDownLatch(1)
64	    try {
65	        val futures = (0 until threads).map { i ->
66	            pool.submit(Callable {
67	                ready.countDown()
68	                start.await()
69	                action(i)
70	            })
71	        }
72	        ready.await()
73	        start.countDown()
74	        return futures.map { runCatching { it.get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } }
75	    } finally {
76	        pool.shutdownNow()
77	    }
78	}
79	```
80	
81	**Why a gate at all:** starting 50 threads one by one in a loop spreads them out in time. The
82	first threads may finish before the last ones start, and then there's no race to test. The gate
83	makes them all wait at the same line and releases them together.
84	
85	**Java concurrency: `CountDownLatch`.** A counter threads can wait on. `countDown()` decrements
86	it; `await()` blocks until it reaches zero. There are two latches here:
87	
88	1. `ready` starts at `threads`. Each worker counts it down as it arrives, and the test thread's
89	   `ready.await()` returns once all of them are waiting.
90	2. `start` starts at 1. Every worker blocks on `start.await()`. The test's single
91	   `start.countDown()` releases all of them at once.
92	
93	**Java concurrency: thread pool and futures.** `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)` makes one
94	thread per worker, so all of them can wait at the gate together (a smaller pool would deadlock:
95	the queued tasks could never arrive at `ready`). `submit` returns a `Future`; `get(30, SECONDS)`
96	waits for its result and rethrows anything the task threw, wrapped in an `ExecutionException`.
97	The timeout makes a hung test fail instead of running forever. `shutdownNow()` in `finally`
98	stops the threads even when something failed.
99	
100	**Kotlin: a generic function.** `fun <T> race(..., action: (Int) -> T): List<Result<T>>` works for
101	any result type. `T` is whatever `action` returns: `InventoryItem?` for `addStock`,
102	`PurchaseResult` for `removeStock`, a `Pair` or an `Int` in the purchase races below. Java writes it the same way: `<T> List<Result<T>> race(...)`.
103	
104	**Kotlin: function types.** `action: (Int) -> T` is a parameter that holds a function taking an
105	`Int` (the thread's index) and returning a `T`. Java would use `IntFunction<T>` or
106	`Function<Integer, T>`. The call sites pass a trailing lambda: `race(threads) { i -> ... }`.
107	
108	**Kotlin: `Callable { ... }`.** `submit` is overloaded for `Runnable` (no result) and `Callable`
109	(returns a result). Writing `Callable { ... }` picks the one that returns a value. This is a SAM
110	conversion, like the row mapper in [InventoryRepository.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md).
111	
112	**Kotlin: ranges.** `0 until threads` is `0, 1, ..., threads - 1` (the end is excluded), and
113	`.map { i -> ... }` turns each index into a submitted task. Java: `IntStream.range(0, threads)`.
114	
115	**Kotlin: `runCatching` and `Result`.** `runCatching { block }` runs the block and returns a
116	`Result`: a success holding the value, or a failure holding the exception. Nothing is thrown.
117	That lets the test collect *every* thread's outcome first, then assert on all of them together.
118	`exceptionOrNull()` and `getOrNull()` read the two sides. Java has no built-in equivalent; you'd
119	catch the exception in a loop and keep it in a list.
120	
121	### The new-SKU creation race
122	
123	```kotlin
124	@RepeatedTest(5)
125	fun `concurrent first-time adds for a new SKU all succeed and sum up`() {
126	    val threads = 50
127	
128	    val results = race(threads) { i -> inventoryRepository.addStock("new-sku", i + 1) }
129	
130	    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
131	    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "adds failed: $failures")
132	    assertTrue(results.all { it.getOrNull() != null }, "an add returned null (treated as overflow)")
133	    assertEquals((1..threads).sum(), quantityOf("new-sku"))
134	}
135	```
136	
137	**What it catches:** the naive way to "create or add" takes two steps. First check whether the
138	row exists, then either `INSERT` or `UPDATE`. Two threads can both see "no row" and both
139	`INSERT`. The second one fails with a duplicate-key error (the primary key), and its stock is
140	lost. A single `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` statement can't split like that: Postgres
141	handles the conflict inside the one statement.
142	
143	**Why each thread adds a different amount (`i + 1`):** if every thread added the same amount,
144	losing one add and double-counting another would cancel out. With 1, 2, ..., 50 the expected
145	total is `(1..50).sum()` = 1275, and a lost or repeated add shows up in the final number.
146	
147	**Kotlin: `mapNotNull`, `all`, `sum`.** `mapNotNull` maps each element and drops the `null`s,
148	leaving only the exceptions. `all { }` is `true` if the condition holds for every element.
149	`(1..threads).sum()` adds up an inclusive range (`..` includes the end, `until` doesn't).
150	
151	**Kotlin: assertion messages.** The last argument of `assertTrue` is the message printed on
152	failure. `"adds failed: $failures"` shows *which* exceptions happened, which beats a bare
153	"expected true".
154	
155	**JUnit: `@RepeatedTest(5)`.** Runs the test five times, each a separate result with its own
156	`@BeforeEach`. Races are intermittent; a broken implementation might pass once by luck, but
157	rarely five times in a row.

159	### The lost-update race
160	
161	```kotlin
162	@RepeatedTest(5)
163	fun `concurrent adds to an existing SKU are never lost`() {
164	    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', 10)").update()
165	    val threads = 50
166	
167	    val results = race(threads) { inventoryRepository.addStock("widget", 2) }
168	
169	    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
170	    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "adds failed: $failures")
171	    assertEquals(10 + threads * 2, quantityOf("widget"))
172	}
173	```
174

176	threads that both read 10 both write 12, and one add disappears. That's a *lost update*. With
177	`SET quantity = inventory.quantity + EXCLUDED.quantity`, Postgres does the read and the write
178	under a row lock inside one statement, so the second thread waits and then adds to 12.
179	
180	**Kotlin: an implicit lambda parameter.** `race(threads) { inventoryRepository.addStock(...) }`
181	doesn't use the index, so the lambda declares no parameter. A lambda with one parameter can
182	leave it out; if needed, it's available as `it`.

184	### The same-SKU purchase race
185	
186	```kotlin
187	// Why: the "remaining" values prove each unit was sold exactly once. Two buyers who both read
188	// stock 10 and wrote 9 would both see 9, and 0..9 would not come back as a clean set.
189	/**
190	 * Same-SKU purchase race: with stock S and N > S buyers of 1, exactly S succeed, N - S are refused
191	 * as insufficient stock, and the SKU ends at 0, never negative.
192	 */
193	@RepeatedTest(5)
194	fun `concurrent purchases never sell more than the stock`() {
195	    val stock = 10
196	    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', ?)").param(stock).update()
197	    val threads = 50
198	
199	    val results = race(threads) { inventoryRepository.removeStock("widget", 1) }
200	
201	    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
202	    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "purchases failed: $failures")
203	    val outcomes = results.map { it.getOrThrow() }
204	    val remaining = outcomes.filterIsInstance<PurchaseResult.Purchased>().map { it.item.quantity }.sorted()
205	    assertEquals((0 until stock).toList(), remaining)
206	    assertEquals(threads - stock, outcomes.count { it == PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock })
207	    assertEquals(0, quantityOf("widget"))
208	}
209	```
210	
211	**What it catches:** the oversell itself. The naive purchase reads the stock, checks
212	`stock >= quantity` in Kotlin, then writes `stock - quantity`. Between the read and the write,
213	another buyer can do the same, and both sell the same last unit. The conditional
214	`UPDATE ... WHERE quantity >= :quantity` does the check and the write in one statement under a row
215	lock, so the second buyer waits and then re-checks against the new value.
216	
217	**Why `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` wouldn't catch the naive version (walkthrough, 2026-09-29):** the
218	naive code writes an absolute value (`SET quantity = 9`), not a relative one. Picture twelve buyers
219	who all read 10 at once:
220	
221	| | Buyers 1–12 (together) | Buyer 13 (a moment later) |
222	| --- | --- | --- |
223	| Read | all read `10` | reads `9` |
224	| Kotlin check | `10 >= 1` passes for all | passes |
225	| Write | all run `SET quantity = 9` | `SET quantity = 8` |
226	| Returned | twelve `Purchased(widget, 9)` | `Purchased(widget, 8)` |
227	
228	More than 10 units are "sold", yet every value written is `>= 0`, so the constraint never fires.
229	The stock can even end *above* 0. The constraint protects "stock is never negative", not "every
230	unit is sold once". Assertion 1 below is the one that fails first.
231	
232	**Three assertions, three kinds of bug:**
233	
234	1. `remaining == [0, 1, ..., 9]`: each successful buyer saw a *different* remaining quantity, so
235	   each of the 10 units was sold exactly once. A lost update would show a repeated value.
236	2. Exactly `threads - stock` (40) were refused as `InsufficientStock`, and none were reported as
237	   `SkuNotFound`, which would be the wrong error for a SKU that exists.
238	3. The final quantity is 0: not negative (oversold) and not above 0 (a buyer refused while stock
239	   remained).
240	
241	**Kotlin: `getOrThrow()`.** Reads a `Result`'s value, or rethrows its exception. It's safe here
242	because the line before already asserted there are no failures.
243	
244	**Kotlin: `filterIsInstance<T>()`.** Keeps only the elements that are a `T`, *and* gives back a
245	`List<T>`, so `it.item` compiles without a cast. It's the list version of the smart cast after
246	`is`. Java: `.filter(x -> x instanceof Purchased).map(x -> (Purchased) x)`.
247	
248	**Kotlin: comparing to a `data object`.** `it == PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock` works because a
249	`data object` is a single instance with a generated `equals`. `count { ... }` counts the elements
250	that match.

256	fun `concurrent purchases of different sizes never oversell`() {

300	    val initial = 20
301	    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', ?)").param(initial).update()
302	    val threads = 60

307	            3
308	        } else {
309	            when (inventoryRepository.removeStock("widget", 5)) {
310	                is PurchaseResult.Purchased -> -5
311	                PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock -> 0
312	                PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound -> error("an existing SKU was reported missing")
313	            }

```kotlin
// Why: a start gate. Every thread first checks in on `ready`, then waits on `start`; releasing
// `start` once makes them all hit the database together instead of one after another.
private fun <T> race(threads: Int, action: (Int) -> T): List<Result<T>> {
    val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)
    val ready = CountDownLatch(threads)
    val start = CountDownLatch(1)
    try {
        val futures = (0 until threads).map { i ->
            pool.submit(Callable {
                ready.countDown()
                start.await()
                action(i)
            })
        }
        ready.await()
        start.countDown()
        return futures.map { runCatching { it.get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } }
    } finally {
        pool.shutdownNow()
    }
}
```

first threads may finish before the last ones start, and then there's no race to test. The gate
makes them all wait at the same line and releases them together.

1. `ready` starts at `threads`. Each worker counts it down as it arrives, and the test thread's
   `ready.await()` returns once all of them are waiting.
2. `start` starts at 1. Every worker blocks on `start.await()`. The test's single
   `start.countDown()` releases all of them at once.

**Java concurrency: thread pool and futures.** `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)` makes one
thread per worker, so all of them can wait at the gate together (a smaller pool would deadlock:
the queued tasks could never arrive at `ready`). `submit` returns a `Future`; `get(30, SECONDS)`
waits for its result and rethrows anything the task threw, wrapped in an `ExecutionException`.
The timeout makes a hung test fail instead of running forever. `shutdownNow()` in `finally`
stops the threads even when something failed.

**Kotlin: a generic function.** `fun <T> race(..., action: (Int) -> T): List<Result<T>>` works for
any result type. `T` is whatever `action` returns: `InventoryItem?` for `addStock`,
`PurchaseResult` for `removeStock`, a `Pair` or an `Int` in the purchase races below. Java writes it the same way: `<T> List<Result<T>> race(...)`.

**Kotlin: function types.** `action: (Int) -> T` is a parameter that holds a function taking an
`Int` (the thread's index) and returning a `T`. Java would use `IntFunction<T>` or
`Function<Integer, T>`. The call sites pass a trailing lambda: `race(threads) { i -> ... }`.

**Kotlin: `Callable { ... }`.** `submit` is overloaded for `Runnable` (no result) and `Callable`
(returns a result). Writing `Callable { ... }` picks the one that returns a value. This is a SAM
conversion, like the row mapper in [InventoryRepository.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md).

**Kotlin: ranges.** `0 until threads` is `0, 1, ..., threads - 1` (the end is excluded), and
`.map { i -> ... }` turns each index into a submitted task. Java: `IntStream.range(0, threads)`.

**Kotlin: `runCatching` and `Result`.** `runCatching { block }` runs the block and returns a
`Result`: a success holding the value, or a failure holding the exception. Nothing is thrown.
That lets the test collect *every* thread's outcome first, then assert on all of them together.
`exceptionOrNull()` and `getOrNull()` read the two sides. Java has no built-in equivalent; you'd
catch the exception in a loop and keep it in a list.

### The new-SKU creation race

```kotlin
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent first-time adds for a new SKU all succeed and sum up`() {
    val threads = 50

    val results = race(threads) { i -> inventoryRepository.addStock("new-sku", i + 1) }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "adds failed: $failures")
    assertTrue(results.all { it.getOrNull() != null }, "an add returned null (treated as overflow)")
    assertEquals((1..threads).sum(), quantityOf("new-sku"))
}
```

**What it catches:** the naive way to "create or add" takes two steps. First check whether the
row exists, then either `INSERT` or `UPDATE`. Two threads can both see "no row" and both
`INSERT`. The second one fails with a duplicate-key error (the primary key), and its stock is
lost. A single `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` statement can't split like that: Postgres
handles the conflict inside the one statement.

**Why each thread adds a different amount (`i + 1`):** if every thread added the same amount,
losing one add and double-counting another would cancel out. With 1, 2, ..., 50 the expected
total is `(1..50).sum()` = 1275, and a lost or repeated add shows up in the final number.

**Kotlin: `mapNotNull`, `all`, `sum`.** `mapNotNull` maps each element and drops the `null`s,
leaving only the exceptions. `all { }` is `true` if the condition holds for every element.
`(1..threads).sum()` adds up an inclusive range (`..` includes the end, `until` doesn't).

**Kotlin: assertion messages.** The last argument of `assertTrue` is the message printed on
failure. `"adds failed: $failures"` shows *which* exceptions happened, which beats a bare
"expected true".

**JUnit: `@RepeatedTest(5)`.** Runs the test five times, each a separate result with its own
`@BeforeEach`. Races are intermittent; a broken implementation might pass once by luck, but
rarely five times in a row.

### The lost-update race

```kotlin
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent adds to an existing SKU are never lost`() {
    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', 10)").update()
    val threads = 50

    val results = race(threads) { inventoryRepository.addStock("widget", 2) }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "adds failed: $failures")
    assertEquals(10 + threads * 2, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**What it catches:** a read-then-write implementation (read 10, compute 12, write 12). Two
threads that both read 10 both write 12, and one add disappears. That's a *lost update*. With
`SET quantity = inventory.quantity + EXCLUDED.quantity`, Postgres does the read and the write
under a row lock inside one statement, so the second thread waits and then adds to 12.

**Kotlin: an implicit lambda parameter.** `race(threads) { inventoryRepository.addStock(...) }`
doesn't use the index, so the lambda declares no parameter. A lambda with one parameter can
leave it out; if needed, it's available as `it`.

### The same-SKU purchase race

```kotlin
// Why: the "remaining" values prove each unit was sold exactly once. Two buyers who both read
// stock 10 and wrote 9 would both see 9, and 0..9 would not come back as a clean set.
/**
 * Same-SKU purchase race: with stock S and N > S buyers of 1, exactly S succeed, N - S are refused
 * as insufficient stock, and the SKU ends at 0, never negative.
 */
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent purchases never sell more than the stock`() {
    val stock = 10
    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', ?)").param(stock).update()
    val threads = 50

    val results = race(threads) { inventoryRepository.removeStock("widget", 1) }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "purchases failed: $failures")
    val outcomes = results.map { it.getOrThrow() }
    val remaining = outcomes.filterIsInstance<PurchaseResult.Purchased>().map { it.item.quantity }.sorted()
    assertEquals((0 until stock).toList(), remaining)
    assertEquals(threads - stock, outcomes.count { it == PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock })
    assertEquals(0, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**What it catches:** the oversell itself. The naive purchase reads the stock, checks
`stock >= quantity` in Kotlin, then writes `stock - quantity`. Between the read and the write,
another buyer can do the same, and both sell the same last unit. The conditional
`UPDATE ... WHERE quantity >= :quantity` does the check and the write in one statement under a row
lock, so the second buyer waits and then re-checks against the new value.

**Why `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` wouldn't catch the naive version (walkthrough, 2026-09-29):** the
naive code writes an absolute value (`SET quantity = 9`), not a relative one. Picture twelve buyers
who all read 10 at once:

| | Buyers 1–12 (together) | Buyer 13 (a moment later) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read | all read `10` | reads `9` |
| Kotlin check | `10 >= 1` passes for all | passes |
| Write | all run `SET quantity = 9` | `SET quantity = 8` |
| Returned | twelve `Purchased(widget, 9)` | `Purchased(widget, 8)` |

More than 10 units are "sold", yet every value written is `>= 0`, so the constraint never fires.
The stock can even end *above* 0. The constraint protects "stock is never negative", not "every
unit is sold once". Assertion 1 below is the one that fails first.

**Three assertions, three kinds of bug:**

1. `remaining == [0, 1, ..., 9]`: each successful buyer saw a *different* remaining quantity, so
   each of the 10 units was sold exactly once. A lost update would show a repeated value.
2. Exactly `threads - stock` (40) were refused as `InsufficientStock`, and none were reported as
   `SkuNotFound`, which would be the wrong error for a SKU that exists.
3. The final quantity is 0: not negative (oversold) and not above 0 (a buyer refused while stock
   remained).

**Kotlin: `getOrThrow()`.** Reads a `Result`'s value, or rethrows its exception. It's safe here
because the line before already asserted there are no failures.

**Kotlin: `filterIsInstance<T>()`.** Keeps only the elements that are a `T`, *and* gives back a
`List<T>`, so `it.item` compiles without a cast. It's the list version of the smart cast after
`is`. Java: `.filter(x -> x instanceof Purchased).map(x -> (Purchased) x)`.

**Kotlin: comparing to a `data object`.** `it == PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock` works because a
`data object` is a single instance with a generated `equals`. `count { ... }` counts the elements
that match.

### Uneven quantities

```kotlin
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent purchases of different sizes never oversell`() {
    val stock = 100
    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', ?)").param(stock).update()
    val threads = 50

    val results = race(threads) { i ->
        val quantity = i % 7 + 1
        quantity to inventoryRepository.removeStock("widget", quantity)
    }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "purchases failed: $failures")
    val outcomes = results.map { it.getOrThrow() }
    assertTrue(outcomes.none { (_, result) -> result == PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound }, "an existing SKU was reported missing")
    val sold = outcomes.filter { (_, result) -> result is PurchaseResult.Purchased }.sumOf { (quantity, _) -> quantity }
    assertTrue(sold <= stock, "sold $sold of $stock")
    assertEquals(stock - sold, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**What it catches:** a check that only works for purchases of 1, for example comparing against
`> 0` instead of `>= :quantity`. The buyers ask for 1 to 7 units (`i % 7 + 1`), about 200 in total
against a stock of 100, so the SKU runs low and a big order can be refused while a small one
still fits.

**Why not assert an exact count:** which buyers win depends on thread timing, so the test asserts
the invariant instead. What was sold never exceeds the stock, and the database agrees exactly with
what the successful buyers were told.

**Kotlin: `to` and `Pair`.** `quantity to result` builds a `Pair(quantity, result)`. `to` is an
*infix* function: called without a dot or parentheses. Each thread returns what it asked for next
to what happened, so the test can add up the successful quantities.

**Kotlin: destructuring in lambdas.** `{ (_, result) -> ... }` unpacks the `Pair` into its two
parts right in the parameter list; `_` skips the part the lambda doesn't need. `sumOf { }` adds up
whatever the lambda returns for each element.

### Restocks mixed with purchases

```kotlin
// Why: demand (30 x 5 = 150) exceeds supply (20 + 30 x 3 = 110), so some purchases are refused
// and the test exercises both outcomes under contention.
@RepeatedTest(5)
fun `concurrent restocks and purchases keep an exact balance`() {
    val initial = 20
    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES ('widget', ?)").param(initial).update()
    val threads = 60

    val results = race(threads) { i ->
        if (i % 2 == 0) {
            checkNotNull(inventoryRepository.addStock("widget", 3)) { "restock refused" }
            3
        } else {
            when (inventoryRepository.removeStock("widget", 5)) {
                is PurchaseResult.Purchased -> -5
                PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock -> 0
                PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound -> error("an existing SKU was reported missing")
            }
        }
    }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "operations failed: $failures")
    assertEquals(initial + results.sumOf { it.getOrThrow() }, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**What it catches:** interference between the two writes. The upsert and the conditional
`UPDATE` both lock the same row; if either did a read-then-write, a restock could overwrite a
purchase (or the other way round) and the books wouldn't balance. Each thread returns its change
to the stock (`+3`, `-5` or `0`), and the final quantity must equal the initial one plus the sum
of the changes.

**Kotlin: `if` and `when` are expressions.** The lambda's last expression is its return value, and
here that's an `if`/`else` whose branches end in `3` or a `when`. In Java both would be
statements, and you'd need a variable or `return`s.

**Kotlin: an exhaustive `when` over a sealed type.** `PurchaseResult` is sealed, so the compiler
knows all its cases. This `when` lists all three and needs no `else`. If someone adds a fourth
case, this code stops compiling until it's handled. `is PurchaseResult.Purchased` checks the type
(a data class, with a new instance each time), while the two objects are compared by value.

**Kotlin: `checkNotNull` and `error`.** `checkNotNull(x) { "msg" }` returns `x` if it isn't null,
otherwise throws `IllegalStateException("msg")`. `error("msg")` always throws one. Inside `race`,
`runCatching` collects that exception, so the `failures` assertion reports it.

# OversellAssertions.kt

> Source: [src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/OversellAssertions.kt](../../../../../src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/OversellAssertions.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-30

## Role

The oversell invariant, written once as a function. After a race of single-unit purchases, it
checks that nothing was oversold. Two tests call it:

- [InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt](InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt.md) runs it against the real
  `InventoryRepository.removeStock` and expects it to **pass**.
- [NegativeControlTest.kt](NegativeControlTest.kt.md) runs it against a naive read-then-write
  purchase and expects it to **fail**.

## Walkthrough

### Why the check is shared

```kotlin
// Why: one shared check, so the negative control proves that the exact assertions guarding the
// real repository can detect an oversell, not a separate check written to fail.
```

**Why:** a negative control is only worth something if it tests the *same* check. If the negative
control had its own assertions, it would only prove that *those* can fail. The real race test
could still have a weak check (say, only "final quantity >= 0", which the naive code passes).
Sharing one function removes that gap.

**Kotlin: a top-level function in the test package.** Like `race` in
[Race.kt](../support/Race.kt.md), it lives directly in the file. It sits in the `inventory`
package, next to the tests, because it works on `PurchaseResult`.

### The precondition

```kotlin
fun assertNoOversell(stock: Int, outcomes: List<PurchaseResult>, finalQuantity: Int?) {
    require(outcomes.size >= stock) { "needs at least $stock buyers, got ${outcomes.size}" }
    assertTrue(outcomes.none { it == PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound }, "an existing SKU was reported missing")
```

**Kotlin: `require` vs. an assertion.** `require` throws `IllegalArgumentException`: *the caller*
used the function wrongly (fewer buyers than units, so "exactly `stock` succeed" can't be
expected). The `assert...` functions throw `AssertionError`: *the code under test* is wrong.
Keeping them apart matters in the negative control, which expects an `AssertionError`, so a
misconfigured test can't pass by accident. `require` was introduced in
[InventoryService.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md).

**Kotlin: `none { }`.** True when no element matches; the opposite of `any { }`.

**Kotlin: comparing to a `data object`.** `it == PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound` works because a
`data object` is a single instance with a generated `equals`.

### The four checks, in order

```kotlin
val remaining = outcomes.filterIsInstance<PurchaseResult.Purchased>().map { it.item.quantity }.sorted()
assertTrue(remaining.size <= stock, "oversold: ${remaining.size} purchases succeeded for a stock of $stock")
assertEquals((0 until stock).toList(), remaining, "each unit must be sold exactly once")
assertEquals(outcomes.size - stock, outcomes.count { it == PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock }, "refused purchases")
assertEquals(0, finalQuantity, "final quantity")
```

Each check catches a different bug:

1. **Oversold:** more purchases succeeded than there were units. This is the invariant itself,
   so it goes first, and its message starts with `oversold` (the negative control checks for it).
2. **Each unit sold exactly once:** every successful buyer was told a *different* remaining
   quantity, `0, 1, ..., stock - 1`. A lost update shows up as a repeated value.
3. **Refused purchases:** everyone who didn't get a unit got `InsufficientStock`.
4. **Final quantity 0:** not negative, and not above 0 (a buyer refused while stock remained).

**Kotlin: `filterIsInstance<T>()`.** Keeps only the elements that are a `T`, *and* gives back a
`List<T>`, so `it.item` compiles without a cast. It's the list version of the smart cast after
`is`. Java: `.filter(x -> x instanceof Purchased).map(x -> (Purchased) x)`.

**Kotlin: assertion messages.** `kotlin.test`'s `assertEquals(expected, actual, message)` takes the
message last (JUnit's `assertEquals` also takes it last in JUnit 5+). The message is what you read
first when a test fails, so each one names the rule that broke.

## Check your understanding

- Why is the negative control only convincing if it calls this same function?
- Why does the function use `require` for the buyer count but `assertTrue` for everything else?
- The naive purchase has twelve buyers who all read 10 and write 9. Which of the four checks
  would fail? Which one fails first, and why is that the one the negative control looks for?
- Why can't a `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint replace check 1?

# NegativeControlTest.kt

> Source: [src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/NegativeControlTest.kt](../../../../../src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/NegativeControlTest.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-30

## Role

The **negative control** from the oversell test plan in [TODO.md](../../../../../.claude/TODO.md).
A green race test only means something if it would go red on broken code. This class feeds a
deliberately naive purchase through the same race and the same check
([OversellAssertions.kt](OversellAssertions.kt.md)) as
[InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt](InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt.md), and asserts that the check fails.

The naive purchase, `NaiveInventoryRepository`, lives in `src/test`, so it never ships. Robert
wrote it (decided 2026-09-30).

## Walkthrough

### Setup

```kotlin
@SpringBootTest
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
class NegativeControlTest @Autowired constructor(
    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
) {

    private val stock = 10
    private val buyers = 12
```

**Spring:** a full context with no test transaction, for the same reason as
`InventoryConcurrencyTest` (see its notes on per-thread transactions). The naive repository is not
a Spring bean. The test builds it with `NaiveInventoryRepository(jdbcClient) { ... }`, so each test
picks its own pause.

**Why 12 buyers for 10 units:** it's the scenario from the purchase walkthrough's last question.
There are more buyers than units, so a correct purchase must refuse two of them.

### Control 1: the naive code works without a race

```kotlin
/** Without concurrency the naive code is correct, so a failure below comes from the race alone. */
@Test
fun `the naive purchase passes the oversell check when buyers take turns`() {
    val naive = NaiveInventoryRepository(jdbcClient) {}

    val outcomes = (1..buyers).map { naive.removeStock("widget", 1) }

    assertNoOversell(stock, outcomes, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**Why:** without this test, the next one could "catch" a naive repository that is simply buggy
(say, it subtracts 2). Passing here pins the blame for the failure below on concurrency alone.

**Kotlin: an empty lambda.** `{}` is a function that takes nothing and does nothing: no pause
between the read and the write. It's written after the parentheses, as a trailing lambda.

**Kotlin: `(1..buyers).map { ... }`.** Runs the purchase twelve times, one after another on the
test thread, and collects the results in a list.

### Control 2: the check catches the race

```kotlin
// Why: a real race only sometimes interleaves badly. The barrier holds every buyer between its
// read and its write until all of them have read, so the lost update happens on every run.
...
@Test
fun `the oversell check catches a naive purchase under a race`() {
    val barrier = CyclicBarrier(buyers)
    val naive = NaiveInventoryRepository(jdbcClient) { barrier.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS) }

    val results = race(buyers) { naive.removeStock("widget", 1) }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "the naive purchases raised errors: $failures")
    val outcomes = results.map { it.getOrThrow() }
    val caught = assertFailsWith<AssertionError> {
        assertNoOversell(stock, outcomes, quantityOf("widget"))
    }
    assertTrue(caught.message.orEmpty().startsWith("oversold"), "expected an oversell, got: ${caught.message}")
}
```

**Java concurrency: `CyclicBarrier`.** A meeting point for a fixed number of threads. Each thread
calls `await()` and blocks until all `buyers` threads have arrived; then all of them continue at
once. Compare the `CountDownLatch` in [Race.kt](../support/Race.kt.md): a latch is counted down by
anyone and opened once, while a barrier is where the waiting threads themselves meet (and it can be
reused, hence "cyclic"). The 10-second timeout turns a stuck thread into a
`TimeoutException` instead of a hang.

**Why the barrier sits between the read and the write:** `race` only makes the buyers *start*
together. Whether two of them then land between each other's read and write is luck. The barrier
removes the luck: no buyer writes until every buyer has read `10`. Then all twelve pass the Kotlin
check and all twelve write `9`. The test is deterministic, so it can't flake.

**What the test proves:**

- No errors: the naive code raises nothing, and the database's `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` never
  fires, because every value written (`9`) is valid on its own.
- The oversell check fails, and its **first** assertion ("oversold: 12 purchases succeeded for a
  stock of 10") is the one that trips.

**Kotlin: `assertFailsWith<T> { }`.** Runs the block and passes only if it throws a `T`; it returns
the exception so you can inspect it. JUnit's Java equivalent is
`assertThrows(AssertionError.class, () -> ...)`. The reified type parameter `<AssertionError>`
replaces the `.class` argument.

**Kotlin: `orEmpty()`.** `caught.message` is a `String?`. `orEmpty()` turns `null` into `""`, so
`startsWith` can be called without a null check.

## Check your understanding

- What would it mean if control 1 failed? Why is it there at all?
- Without the `CyclicBarrier`, would control 2 still pass every time? What would you see instead?
- Why does the naive code never trigger `CHECK (quantity >= 0)`?
- `CountDownLatch` vs. `CyclicBarrier`: which one does `race` use, which one does the naive

## Role

The **negative control** from the oversell test plan in [TODO.md](../../../../../.claude/TODO.md).
A green race test only means something if it would go red on broken code. This class feeds a
deliberately naive purchase through the same race and the same check
([OversellAssertions.kt](OversellAssertions.kt.md)) as
[InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt](InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt.md), and asserts that the check fails.

The naive purchase, `NaiveInventoryRepository`, lives in `src/test`, so it never ships. Robert
wrote it (decided 2026-09-30).

## Walkthrough

### Setup

```kotlin
@SpringBootTest
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
class NegativeControlTest @Autowired constructor(
    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
) {

    private val stock = 10
    private val buyers = 12
```

**Spring:** a full context with no test transaction, for the same reason as
`InventoryConcurrencyTest` (see its notes on per-thread transactions). The naive repository is not
a Spring bean. The test builds it with `NaiveInventoryRepository(jdbcClient) { ... }`, so each test
picks its own pause.

**Why 12 buyers for 10 units:** it's the scenario from the purchase walkthrough's last question.
There are more buyers than units, so a correct purchase must refuse two of them.

### Control 1: the naive code works without a race

```kotlin
/** Without concurrency the naive code is correct, so a failure below comes from the race alone. */
@Test
fun `the naive purchase passes the oversell check when buyers take turns`() {
    val naive = NaiveInventoryRepository(jdbcClient) {}

    val outcomes = (1..buyers).map { naive.removeStock("widget", 1) }

    assertNoOversell(stock, outcomes, quantityOf("widget"))
}
```

**Why:** without this test, the next one could "catch" a naive repository that is simply buggy
(say, it subtracts 2). Passing here pins the blame for the failure below on concurrency alone.

**Kotlin: an empty lambda.** `{}` is a function that takes nothing and does nothing: no pause
between the read and the write. It's written after the parentheses, as a trailing lambda.

**Kotlin: `(1..buyers).map { ... }`.** Runs the purchase twelve times, one after another on the
test thread, and collects the results in a list.

### Control 2: the check catches the race

```kotlin
// Why: a real race only sometimes interleaves badly. The barrier holds every buyer between its
// read and its write until all of them have read, so the lost update happens on every run.
...
@Test
fun `the oversell check catches a naive purchase under a race`() {
    val barrier = CyclicBarrier(buyers)
    val naive = NaiveInventoryRepository(jdbcClient) { barrier.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS) }

    val results = race(buyers) { naive.removeStock("widget", 1) }

    val failures = results.mapNotNull { it.exceptionOrNull() }
    assertTrue(failures.isEmpty(), "the naive purchases raised errors: $failures")
    val outcomes = results.map { it.getOrThrow() }
    val caught = assertFailsWith<AssertionError> {
        assertNoOversell(stock, outcomes, quantityOf("widget"))
    }
    assertTrue(caught.message.orEmpty().startsWith("oversold"), "expected an oversell, got: ${caught.message}")
}
```

**Java concurrency: `CyclicBarrier`.** A meeting point for a fixed number of threads. Each thread
calls `await()` and blocks until all `buyers` threads have arrived; then all of them continue at
once. Compare the `CountDownLatch` in [Race.kt](../support/Race.kt.md): a latch is counted down by
anyone and opened once, while a barrier is where the waiting threads themselves meet (and it can be
reused, hence "cyclic"). The 10-second timeout turns a stuck thread into a
`TimeoutException` instead of a hang.

**Why the barrier sits between the read and the write:** `race` only makes the buyers *start*
together. Whether two of them then land between each other's read and write is luck. The barrier
removes the luck: no buyer writes until every buyer has read `10`. Then all twelve pass the Kotlin
check and all twelve write `9`. The test is deterministic, so it can't flake.

  fires, because every value written (`9`) is valid on its own.

  stock of 10") is the one that trips.

the exception so you can inspect it. JUnit's Java equivalent is
`assertThrows(AssertionError.class, () -> ...)`. The reified type parameter `<AssertionError>`
replaces the `.class` argument.

**Kotlin: `orEmpty()`.** `caught.message` is a `String?`. `orEmpty()` turns `null` into `""`, so

> Source: [src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/OversellAssertions.kt](../../../../../src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/OversellAssertions.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-30

## Role

The oversell invariant, written once as a function. After a race of single-unit purchases, it
checks that nothing was oversold. Two tests call it:

- [InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt](InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt.md) runs it against the real
  `InventoryRepository.removeStock` and expects it to **pass**.
- [NegativeControlTest.kt](NegativeControlTest.kt.md) runs it against a naive read-then-write
  purchase and expects it to **fail**.

## Walkthrough

### Why the check is shared

```kotlin
// Why: one shared check, so the negative control proves that the exact assertions guarding the
// real repository can detect an oversell, not a separate check written to fail.
```

**Why:** a negative control is only worth something if it tests the *same* check. If the negative
control had its own assertions, it would only prove that *those* can fail. The real race test
could still have a weak check (say, only "final quantity >= 0", which the naive code passes).
Sharing one function removes that gap.

**Kotlin: a top-level function in the test package.** Like `race` in
[Race.kt](../support/Race.kt.md), it lives directly in the file. It sits in the `inventory`
package, next to the tests, because it works on `PurchaseResult`.

### The precondition

```kotlin
fun assertNoOversell(stock: Int, outcomes: List<PurchaseResult>, finalQuantity: Int?) {
    require(outcomes.size >= stock) { "needs at least $stock buyers, got ${outcomes.size}" }
    assertTrue(outcomes.none { it == PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound }, "an existing SKU was reported missing")
```

**Kotlin: `require` vs. an assertion.** `require` throws `IllegalArgumentException`: *the caller*
used the function wrongly (fewer buyers than units, so "exactly `stock` succeed" can't be
expected). The `assert...` functions throw `AssertionError`: *the code under test* is wrong.
Keeping them apart matters in the negative control, which expects an `AssertionError`, so a
misconfigured test can't pass by accident. `require` was introduced in
[InventoryService.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md).

**Kotlin: `none { }`.** True when no element matches; the opposite of `any { }`.

**Kotlin: comparing to a `data object`.** `it == PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound` works because a
`data object` is a single instance with a generated `equals`.

### The four checks, in order

```kotlin
val remaining = outcomes.filterIsInstance<PurchaseResult.Purchased>().map { it.item.quantity }.sorted()
assertTrue(remaining.size <= stock, "oversold: ${remaining.size} purchases succeeded for a stock of $stock")
assertEquals((0 until stock).toList(), remaining, "each unit must be sold exactly once")
assertEquals(outcomes.size - stock, outcomes.count { it == PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock }, "refused purchases")
assertEquals(0, finalQuantity, "final quantity")
```

Each check catches a different bug:

1. **Oversold:** more purchases succeeded than there were units. This is the invariant itself,
   so it goes first, and its message starts with `oversold` (the negative control checks for it).
2. **Each unit sold exactly once:** every successful buyer was told a *different* remaining
   quantity, `0, 1, ..., stock - 1`. A lost update shows up as a repeated value.
3. **Refused purchases:** everyone who didn't get a unit got `InsufficientStock`.
4. **Final quantity 0:** not negative, and not above 0 (a buyer refused while stock remained).

**Kotlin: `filterIsInstance<T>()`.** Keeps only the elements that are a `T`, *and* gives back a
`List<T>`, so `it.item` compiles without a cast. It's the list version of the smart cast after
`is`. Java: `.filter(x -> x instanceof Purchased).map(x -> (Purchased) x)`.

**Kotlin: assertion messages.** `kotlin.test`'s `assertEquals(expected, actual, message)` takes the
message last (JUnit's `assertEquals` also takes it last in JUnit 5+). The message is what you read
first when a test fails, so each one names the rule that broke.

## Check your understanding

- Why is the negative control only convincing if it calls this same function?
- Why does the function use `require` for the buyer count but `assertTrue` for everything else?
- The naive purchase has twelve buyers who all read 10 and write 9. Which of the four checks
  would fail? Which one fails first, and why is that the one the negative control looks for?
- Why can't a `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint replace check 1?

-| `throw` as an expression, `Nothing` | `x ?: throw E()` has the non-null type of `x`; `Nothing` fits any type | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |

-| KDoc block tags (`@throws`) | Tags start their own line; `@throws` is how a signature announces an exception without checked exceptions | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |

-| Plain constructor parameters | No `val`/`var` = usable only during construction, not a property | [SkuNotFoundException.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/SkuNotFoundException.kt.md) |

-| Array literals in annotations | `@ValueSource(ints = [0, -5])`; Java writes `{0, -5}` | [InventoryControllerTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt.md) |

-| Class with no constructor parameters | `class E : RuntimeException("msg")`, created with `E()` | [AddStockOverflowException.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/AddStockOverflowException.kt.md) |

+| Final by default | Classes and functions are `final` unless `open`; the `plugin.spring` compiler plugin opens Spring beans | [build.gradle.kts](notes/build.gradle.kts.md) |

+| Final is not immutable | `open`/`final` controls subclassing and overriding; `val`/`var` controls mutability. A final method under a Spring proxy fails silently | [build.gradle.kts](notes/build.gradle.kts.md) |
+| Platform types and `-Xjsr305=strict` | How Java nullability annotations become real `T` / `T?` types | [build.gradle.kts](notes/build.gradle.kts.md) |
+| Class with no body | `class InventoryApplication` needs no braces | [InventoryApplication.kt](notes/main/InventoryApplication.kt.md) |
+| Top-level functions | `fun main` lives outside any class; compiled into `InventoryApplicationKt` | [InventoryApplication.kt](notes/main/InventoryApplication.kt.md) |
+| Reified type parameters | `runApplication<T>()`, `withType<Test>`: the type in `<>` instead of `T::class.java` | [InventoryApplication.kt](notes/main/InventoryApplication.kt.md) |
+| Spread operator `*` | Pass an array's elements as a vararg | [InventoryApplication.kt](notes/main/InventoryApplication.kt.md) |
+| Named arguments | `proxyBeanMethods = false`, also in annotations | [TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](notes/test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md) |
+| Expression bodies | `fun f(): T = expr` instead of `{ return expr }` | [TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](notes/test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md) |
+| Class references `X::class` | Kotlin's version of Java's `X.class` | [InventoryApplicationTests.kt](notes/test/InventoryApplicationTests.kt.md) |
+| `internal` vs package-private | Kotlin has no package-private; `internal` = same Gradle module | [README](../../README.md#project-layout) |
+| Public by default | No modifier means `public` (Java: package-private); helpers must say `private` | [InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md) |
+| `@Autowired constructor` | Annotating the primary constructor needs the `constructor` keyword | [InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md) |
+| Backtick function names | `` fun `reads like a sentence`() `` for test names | [InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md) |
+| Extension functions | `fun MockMvc.get(...)`: a function added to a class from outside it | [InventoryControllerTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt.md) |
+| Raw strings `"""` | Multi-line strings without escaping; `trimIndent()` to strip indentation | [InventoryControllerTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt.md) |
+| Primary constructor properties | `class X(private val dep: Dep)`: declares and assigns a property in the constructor | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |
+| Read-only `List` vs `MutableList` | `List` has no `add`/`remove`; callers get a snapshot | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |

+| Lambdas, `_` and SAM conversion | `{ rs, _ -> ... }` stands in for Java's single-method `RowMapper`; `_` = unused parameter | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |

+| A lambda's last expression is its return value | `.query { }` / `.map { }` call the lambda once per element and collect what it returns | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |
+| KDoc vs `// Why:` | KDoc (`/** */`) says what, for callers, shown on hover; `// Why:` says why, for maintainers | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |

+| JSpecify nullability from Java | Spring 7's `@Nullable` makes `query(Class)` yield `T?`; a row-mapper lambda keeps `T` non-null | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |
+| `data class` | Generated `equals`/`hashCode`/`toString`/`copy`/`componentN` from constructor properties; Kotlin's Java `record` | [InventoryItem.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryItem.kt.md) |

+| `==` vs `===`, and `copy` | `==` calls `equals` (value equality for data classes); `===` is identity. `copy` returns a new object and leaves the original alone | [InventoryItem.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryItem.kt.md) |
+| No checked exceptions | Kotlin has no `throws` clause; unchecked `DataAccessException` travels up to a `500` | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |

+| Nullable types `T?` | `InventoryItem?` = an item or `null`; the compiler makes you handle `null` before use. Kotlin's built-in `Optional` | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |

+| `singleOrNull` / `single` / `firstOrNull` | Zero-or-one lookups on a list; `singleOrNull` returns `null` (no exception) for 0 *or* 2+ elements | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |
+| Elvis operator `?:` | `a ?: b` = `a` unless it's `null`, then `b` | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |
+| `throw` as an expression, `Nothing` | `x ?: throw E()` has the non-null type of `x`; `Nothing` fits any type | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |

+| KDoc block tags (`@throws`) | Tags start their own line; `@throws` is how a signature announces an exception without checked exceptions | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |
+| Extending a class | `class A(x: T) : B(...)` = `extends B` plus the `super(...)` call | [SkuNotFoundException.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/SkuNotFoundException.kt.md) |
+| Plain constructor parameters | No `val`/`var` = usable only during construction, not a property | [SkuNotFoundException.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/SkuNotFoundException.kt.md) |

+| Storage vs visibility | `val` decides whether a constructor parameter is kept; `private` decides who can read it. `private val` enforces the layers | [SkuNotFoundException.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/SkuNotFoundException.kt.md) |
+| No ternary; `if` is an expression | Java's `c ? a : b` is `if (c) a else b`; `?:` (Elvis) only tests for `null` | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |
+| String templates | `"SKU not found: $skuId"`, and `${expr}` for anything longer than a name | [SkuNotFoundException.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/SkuNotFoundException.kt.md) |
+| Nullable values from Java | `Throwable.message` is `String?` because `getMessage()` may return null | [InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) |
+| Default arguments | `fun f(x: T = default)`: callers may leave the argument out; replaces Java overloads | [InventoryControllerTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt.md) |
+| Array literals in annotations | `@ValueSource(ints = [0, -5])`; Java writes `{0, -5}` | [InventoryControllerTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt.md) |
+| Generic functions and function types | `fun <T> race(action: (Int) -> T)`: a type parameter plus a parameter that holds a function | [Race.kt](notes/test/support/Race.kt.md) |
+| Ranges `..` and `until` | `1..n` includes `n`, `0 until n` excludes it; both work with `map`, `sum` | [Race.kt](notes/test/support/Race.kt.md) |
+| `runCatching` and `Result` | Runs a block and captures success or exception as a value, nothing thrown | [Race.kt](notes/test/support/Race.kt.md) |
+| Implicit lambda parameter `it` | A one-parameter lambda can leave the parameter out and use `it` | [InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt.md) |

+| Safe-call operator `?.` | `a?.b` is `null` instead of an NPE when `a` is `null`; chains end in one `?:` fallback | [InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) |
+| `require` / `check` | `require(cond) { msg }` throws `IllegalArgumentException`; the message lambda runs only on failure | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |

+| Block body vs expression body | `= expr` holds one expression; two steps (check, then act) read better as `{ }` with an explicit `return` | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |
+| Class with no constructor parameters | `class E : RuntimeException("msg")`, created with `E()` | [AddStockOverflowException.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/AddStockOverflowException.kt.md) |

+| Sealed interfaces | `sealed interface` closes the list of implementations (same package + module), so a `when` over it can be exhaustive; Java 17's `sealed ... permits` | [PurchaseResult.kt](notes/main/inventory/PurchaseResult.kt.md) |
+| `object` and `data object` | A class with exactly one instance, used by name without `()`; `data` adds a readable `toString` | [PurchaseResult.kt](notes/main/inventory/PurchaseResult.kt.md) |

+| Nested classes | A class declared inside another is referenced as `Outer.Inner`; like a Java `static` nested class unless marked `inner` | [PurchaseResult.kt](notes/main/inventory/PurchaseResult.kt.md) |

+| `when` without a subject | `when { cond -> value }`: an `if`/`else if` chain, checked top to bottom, `else` required when used as a value | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |

+| Smart casts | After `x != null` or `x is T`, the compiler treats a variable nothing can change in between (e.g. a local `val`) as the narrower type in that branch | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |

+| `Int::class.java` vs `javaObjectType` | `.java` is the primitive `int.class`, `.javaObjectType` the boxed `Integer.class` (can hold `null`) | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |
+| KDoc links `[Name]` | Square brackets in KDoc link to a declaration; Javadoc's `{@link}` | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |

+| `when` with a subject, `is` and exhaustiveness | `when (val x = ...) { is A -> ...; B -> ... }`: type checks and equality; no `else` needed over a sealed type | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md#purchaseinventory-one-branch-per-outcome) |

+| `orEmpty()` | Turns a `null` `String?` into `""` so it can be used without a null check | [NegativeControlTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/NegativeControlTest.kt.md) |

+| `return` and a line break | A line break after a bare `return` ends the statement; the value has to start on the same line | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md#purchaseinventory-one-branch-per-outcome) |

content.text:
A negative control is a **test of your tests**.

## The problem it solves

`InventoryConcurrencyTest` is green: 50 buyers race for 10 units and nothing oversells. But green only means something if the test **could** have gone red. There are two ways it could be green:

1. `removeStock` really is safe under concurrency.
2. The test can't see an oversell. Maybe the race never overlaps, or the assertions are too weak, e.g. only checking "final quantity ≥ 0".

From outside, those two look the same. The negative control rules out #2: feed the test code we **know** is broken and confirm it goes red.

The term comes from lab science. You run the experiment on a sample you know has no effect, to prove your instrument isn't just always reading "positive". Here the instrument is `assertNoOversell`, and the known-bad sample is your naive repository.

## The case: a lost update

The broken code is the naive purchase you described in the walkthrough:

```
read quantity        →  10
check in Kotlin      →  10 >= 1, ok
write absolute value →  SET quantity = 9
```

Each step is fine alone. The bug is the gap between the read and the write. With 12 buyers and 10 units:

| | Buyers 1–12 |
|---|---|
| Read | all read `10` |
| Kotlin check | all pass |
| Write | all write `9` |
| Told | 12 × "Purchased, 9 left" |

Twelve sales from a stock of 10, and the database ends at **9**, not 0. No exception is thrown. `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` never fires, because 9 is a perfectly valid number. That's why this bug is dangerous: the only way to catch it is an assertion that counts what was sold.

## Why two tests

**Test 1, buyers take turns:** the naive code runs 12 times, one after another. It behaves correctly: 10 sold, 2 refused, ends at 0, and the check passes. That proves your naive code isn't simply buggy (subtracting wrong, say). Any failure in test 2 is caused by concurrency and nothing else.

**Test 2, buyers race:** same code, same check, but the buyers run at once. Now the check must fail, and it must fail on the "oversold" assertion specifically, not some other assertion error.

## Why the `CyclicBarrier`

A real race is luck. Buyers usually get between each other's read and write, but not always. If the test relied on luck, it could flake. So the barrier, passed in as your `pauseBeforeWrite`, holds every buyer after its read until all 12 have read. Only then does anyone write. That forces the worst-case interleaving on every run, so the test is deterministic.

That's also why `pauseBeforeWrite` is a constructor parameter. Test 1 passes `{}` (no pause), and test 2 passes the barrier. It's the same repository with a different hook.

## Why it's in `src/test`

It's deliberately wrong code. It exists only to be caught, so it must never ship. Keeping it next to the tests makes it permanent proof, not a one-off experiment someone ran once.

**Check yourself:** if you removed the "each unit sold exactly once" assertion from `assertNoOversell`, would test 2 still catch the naive code? What if you also removed the "oversold" one?

Signature: `fun removeStock(skuId: String, quantity: Int): PurchaseResult`, with a one-line KDoc.

1. **Read.** Get the current quantity for `skuId` as an `Int?`. It's null when there's no row. The pattern is `findBySkuId` in `InventoryRepository`: `.sql(...)`, `.param(...)`, `.query { rs, _ -> ... }`, `.list().singleOrNull()`. **One Kotlin detail for step 2:** after `if (current == null) return ...`, the compiler knows `current` is an `Int` from then on. That's the same smart cast you saw with `!= null` in the service, so the comparison in the next check compiles without `!!`.
