# InventoryLoadTest.kt

> Source: [src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryLoadTest.kt](../../../../../src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryLoadTest.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-30

## Role

The **HTTP load test** from the oversell test plan in [TODO.md](../../../../../.claude/TODO.md). The
race tests fire one burst of 50 requests. This one keeps 50 clients buying and restocking three
popular SKUs over real HTTP for 20 seconds, which is tens of thousands of requests. At the end, the
books must balance exactly for every SKU.

It runs with `./gradlew loadTest` (see [build.gradle.kts](../../build.gradle.kts.md#a-separate-task-for-the-load-test)),
not with `./gradlew test`, because it takes a fixed time (decided by Robert, 2026-09-30). It also
prints throughput and latency, so it doubles as a rough performance check.

A 5-second run on 2026-09-30 (a Windows laptop, Postgres in Docker) gave:

```
Load test: 50 clients for 5.0 s
  requests:   12223 (2439 per second)
  purchases:  4225 succeeded, 4418 refused
  restocks:   3580
  latency ms: p50 18.336, p95 38.576, p99 56.805, max 140.117
  final stock: {hot-1=8, hot-2=0, hot-3=3}
```

## Walkthrough

### Setup: a real server on a random port

```kotlin
@Tag("load")
@SpringBootTest(
    webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT,
    // Why: warnings only, so the summary isn't buried under startup logs in the loadTest output.
    properties = ["logging.level.root=WARN"],
)
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class)
class InventoryLoadTest @Autowired constructor(
    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
    @LocalServerPort private val port: Int,
) {
```

**Spring: `WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT`.** By default `@SpringBootTest` has no real server (MockMvc
calls the controllers directly). `RANDOM_PORT` starts the embedded Tomcat on a free port, so the
test talks to it through real sockets with [InventoryHttpClient.kt](../support/InventoryHttpClient.kt.md).
`@LocalServerPort` injects the port that was picked.

**Spring: `properties = [...]`.** Sets properties for this test's context only. Kotlin writes array
arguments of annotations with `[...]`.

**JUnit: `@Tag("load")`.** The label the Gradle tasks filter on.

### Settings from the command line

```kotlin
private val seconds = System.getProperty("load.seconds")?.toLong() ?: 20
private val clients = System.getProperty("load.clients")?.toInt() ?: 50
```

**Kotlin: `?.` and `?:` together.** `System.getProperty` returns `String?`. `?.toLong()` converts it
only if it's there, and `?: 20` supplies the default otherwise. Java would need
`p != null ? Long.parseLong(p) : 20`. The build forwards `-Dload.seconds=...` to the test JVM.

### Each client keeps its own tally

```kotlin
/** What one client did: units sold and received per SKU, outcome counts, and every latency. */
private class Tally {
    val sold = mutableMapOf<String, Int>()
    val received = mutableMapOf<String, Int>()
    var purchased = 0
    var refused = 0
    var restocks = 0
    val latenciesMicros = mutableListOf<Long>()
}
```

**Why per client:** each client writes only to its own `Tally`, so the maps and counters need no
locks or atomics. The tallies are added up once everyone has finished. The only thing the clients
contend on is what's under test: the app and the database.

### The run

```kotlin
val tallies = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { executor ->
    (0 until clients)
        .map { i -> executor.submit(Callable { runClient(client, Random(i), deadline) }) }
        .map { it.get() }
}
```

**Java 21: virtual threads.** `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` runs each task on a *virtual*
thread: a lightweight thread managed by the JVM, not the operating system. A blocked virtual thread
(waiting on HTTP) costs almost nothing, so thousands are fine. The race helper in
[Race.kt](../support/Race.kt.md) uses a fixed pool of platform threads instead, because it needs
exactly N threads waiting at a gate.

**Kotlin: `use`.** Runs the block, then closes the resource, even if the block throws. It's Java's
try-with-resources. Closing this executor waits for its tasks to finish.

**Kotlin: `Random(i)`.** A random generator seeded with the client's number, so each client's
sequence of choices is different but repeatable.

### One client's loop

```kotlin
// Why: each client keeps its own Tally and they're added up at the end, so the clients never
// contend on shared counters, only on the app and the database.
private fun runClient(client: InventoryHttpClient, random: Random, deadline: Long): Tally {
    val tally = Tally()
    while (System.nanoTime() < deadline) {
        val sku = hotSkus.random(random)
        val quantity = random.nextInt(1, 4)
        val start = System.nanoTime()
        if (random.nextInt(100) < 70) {
            when (client.purchase(sku, quantity)) {
                is PurchaseResult.Purchased -> {
                    tally.purchased++
                    tally.sold.merge(sku, quantity, Int::plus)
                }
                PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock -> tally.refused++
                PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound -> error("$sku was reported missing")
            }
        } else {
            client.receive(sku, quantity)
            tally.restocks++
            tally.received.merge(sku, quantity, Int::plus)
        }
        tally.latenciesMicros += (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000
    }
    return tally
}
```

**Why these odds:** 70% purchases against 30% restocks, with the same sizes (1 to 3 units), means
demand outruns supply. Each SKU starts at 100, sells out within the first second or so, and then
spends the rest of the run near zero, with every restock immediately fought over. That's the zone
where an oversell would happen. A test with plenty of stock would never get near the boundary.

**Kotlin: `random.nextInt(1, 4)`** gives 1, 2 or 3; the upper bound is excluded, like `until`.
`hotSkus.random(random)` picks a list element using that generator.

**Kotlin: `merge(key, value, Int::plus)`.** A `MutableMap` method from Java: store `value` if the key
is absent, otherwise combine the old and new value with the function. `Int::plus` is a *function
reference*, the `+` operator as a function. Java: `Integer::sum`.

**Kotlin: `+=` on a list.** `latenciesMicros += x` adds an element to a `MutableList` (`add(x)`).

**Kotlin: `1_000`.** Underscores in number literals are only for readability, as in Java.

### The checks

```kotlin
val stored = client.inventory().associate { it.skuId to it.quantity }
for (sku in hotSkus) {

fun `sustained load on hot SKUs never oversells and keeps an exact balance`() {
    jdbcClient.sql("DELETE FROM inventory").update()
    val client = InventoryHttpClient("http://localhost:$port")
    hotSkus.forEach { client.receive(it, initialStock) }
    val deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(seconds)

    val started = System.nanoTime()
```

**Why seed over HTTP:** the three SKUs start at 100 units each through `POST /inventory/{skuId}`,
the same path a real client would use. The `DELETE` goes straight to the database: no endpoint
deletes, and the table must start empty because the Spring context (and its Postgres) may be
shared with other tests.

**Java: `System.nanoTime()`.** A clock for measuring *durations*, in nanoseconds. Unlike
`currentTimeMillis()`, it never jumps when the system clock is adjusted, so it's the right tool for
deadlines and latencies. `TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(seconds)` converts the run length.
`(System.nanoTime() - started) / 1e9` turns the elapsed time into seconds: `1e9` is a `Double`
literal (10⁹), so the division gives a `Double`, not a truncated `Long`.

The reviewer passed the docs, and I've fixed its two last small items. The TODO is updated and the notes check is clean. That completes every part of the testing feature. The only thing left to commit is the load test and the doc-review fixes.

**What the doc review caught:**
- **My wrong reasoning:**
  - I'd written that `race` *needs* platform threads. In fact virtual threads would work there too.
  - I'd said HTTP/2 upgrades "cost a round trip". They're only extra headers, which Tomcat ignores.
  - "JUnit silently skips" was too strong: since JUnit 5.13 it logs a discovery warning, which Gradle hides.
- **A misleading comment:** a `// Why:` in `InventoryConcurrencyTest` credited the wrong check in the negative control.
- **A stale README line:** it still said `./gradlew test` runs *all* tests. The load test is now excluded from it.
- **Gaps:** about a dozen passages in the notes weren't quoted or explained, and three quotes broke the quoting format. All fixed.

## Proposed commits

**1. `Add HTTP load test with a separate loadTest task`**
- `build.gradle.kts` and its notes
- `InventoryLoadTest` and its notes
- the README test table and build commands
- the concepts index and the TODO

**2. `Fix doc-review findings in the testing notes`**
- the two comment fixes (in `InventoryConcurrencyTest` and `InventoryPropertyTest`)
- the other notes files

Should I commit these?

## Where the feature stands

After those two commits the branch has 8 commits, and the build passes with 124 tests plus `loadTest`. Here's what it added:

| Part | What it proves |
|---|---|
| (a) Negative control | Your `NaiveInventoryRepository` gets caught by the same check that passes the real code. |
| (e) Contract validation | Every response of every endpoint matches `inventory.yaml`, with `InventoryItem` checked strictly. |
| (d) Property-based | 200 random operation sequences agree with an in-memory model; Kotest shrank a broken model's failure to 2 steps. |
| (b) Multi-instance | Two app copies share one database, and nothing oversells because the guarantee lives in Postgres. |
| (c) Load | 50 clients for 20 seconds around 2,000+ requests per second, and the books balance exactly. |

Two things are still open from your earlier list, as their own small tasks:
- **README polish:** the "walkthrough pending" note in the purchase row, purchase `curl` examples, and demo seed data.
- **The `charset=UTF-8` decision.**

Ready for `/walkthrough`, then `/ship`.

**1. Correct.** One more detail: code under `src/test` is never packaged into the jar, so it can't ship by accident.

**2. Half there.** `Unit` is the "void" part: it returns nothing useful. But read the whole type:

- `()`: it takes **no arguments**
- `->`: "returns"
- `Unit`: nothing useful

So `() -> Unit` isn't a value you compute. It's a **function** you're holding. `pauseBeforeWrite` stores *a piece of code*, and `pauseBeforeWrite()` runs it. The test decides what that code is: `{}` does nothing, and `{ barrier.await(...) }` waits for the other buyers.

**3. This one's a mix-up.** `private val` has nothing to do with the return type. It controls whether the constructor argument is **kept** after the object is built. The two words do separate jobs:

| Keyword | Job |
|---|---|
| `val` | **Store** it as a property, so `removeStock` can use it later |
| `private` | Only code inside this class can see that property |

Without `val`, `pauseBeforeWrite` is only a constructor argument. It exists while the object is being built and is gone afterwards. Then the `pauseBeforeWrite()` call on line 32 wouldn't compile: "unresolved reference". It's the same reason `jdbcClient` has `val`: `removeStock` uses both long after construction. In Java terms, `private val x` generates the `private final` field plus the `this.x = x` assignment.

**4. Correct.** The test builds it by hand: `NaiveInventoryRepository(jdbcClient) { ... }`. It passes in the `JdbcClient` bean Spring injected into the test, and the lambda goes after the parentheses because it's the last parameter.

**Chunk 2: `removeStock`** ([NaiveInventoryRepository.kt:17-40](src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/NaiveInventoryRepository.kt#L17-L40)). That's the right walk-through, and six steps is just how I counted them. Two refinements on the gap:

**1. The gap isn't only the pause.** It's everything between the `SELECT` and the `UPDATE`: the Kotlin check, the subtraction, and the pause. Delete `pauseBeforeWrite()` and the gap still exists in production; it's just microseconds wide instead of held open. The pause only makes the bad timing happen on every run instead of occasionally.

**2. "Out of date" understates it. The write itself is destructive.** Picture buyers A and B:

| | Buyer A | Buyer B |
|---|---|---|
| read | 10 | 10 |
| compute | 9 | 9 |
| write | `SET quantity = 9` | `SET quantity = 9` (**erases A's sale**) |

It's not only that A's returned number is stale. B's `SET quantity = 9` **overwrites** A's write, because it's an absolute value computed from an old read. That's the lost update: two units sold, the database says one. And since 9 is a valid number, `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` never objects.

The real `removeStock` closes the gap by putting the check and the write in **one statement**: `UPDATE ... SET quantity = quantity - :q WHERE quantity >= :q`. Postgres locks the row, so B waits and then re-checks against A's result.

# Interview prep

Questions a reviewer might ask in the follow-up interview, with short answers I should be able to
give out loud. Answers are folded: try each question first, then open it to check.

New questions are added during walkthroughs when a topic looks interview-worthy. Longer
explanations live in the [study notes](notes/README.md); each answer links to them.

## Design and failure modes

### What happens if two rows ever share the same SKU?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

`findBySkuId` ends in `.list().singleOrNull()`. With two rows, `singleOrNull()` returns `null`
without throwing. The service then throws `SkuNotFoundException`, and the client gets
**404 "SKU not found: widget"** for a SKU that actually exists twice. That's a silent bug: the API
gives a wrong answer and nothing is logged.

It can't happen today because `sku_id` is the **primary key**, so Postgres rejects a second
`widget` row. The Kotlin code is correct *because of* the database constraint. Keeping the primary
key is the real fix.

If `sku_id` ever stopped being unique, the lookup would need reworking:
- **`.single()`** throws on two rows, so the bug would surface loudly as a 500 instead of a false 404.
  But it also throws on **zero** rows, which is the normal "not found" case, so on its own it would
  turn every missing SKU into a 500.
- A version that handles both cases: `val rows = ...list()`, then `null` when `rows` is empty,
  the item when there's one, and an error (such as `IllegalStateException`) when there are more.

### How do you know your race tests would actually catch an oversell?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

A **negative control**: `NegativeControlTest` runs a deliberately naive purchase
(`NaiveInventoryRepository`: read the stock, check it in Kotlin, write an absolute value) through
the same `race()` and the same `assertNoOversell` that guard the real repository.

- When buyers take turns, the naive code passes the check. So it isn't simply buggy.
- When they race, a `CyclicBarrier` holds every buyer between its read and its write. All 12 read
  10 and all write 9: twelve sales from ten units, the stock ends at 9, and no error is raised
  (9 passes `CHECK (quantity >= 0)`). The check fails on its `oversold` assertion, and the test
  asserts it failed for that reason.

Because the check is **shared**, this proves the exact assertions on the real code can detect a
lost update. See [NegativeControlTest notes](notes/test/inventory/NegativeControlTest.kt.md).
</details>

### Why does the purchase stay correct with several app instances?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The guarantee lives in Postgres, not in the app: one `UPDATE ... SET quantity = quantity - :q
WHERE quantity >= :q` takes a row lock, so a second buyer waits and re-checks against the new value.
A Kotlin-side fix (a `synchronized` block or a per-SKU lock around read-then-write) would pass the
single-app race tests but fail with two instances, because each JVM has its own lock.
`MultiInstanceRaceTest` starts two full app contexts on one database and races buyers across both
over HTTP to prove it. See [MultiInstanceRaceTest notes](notes/test/inventory/MultiInstanceRaceTest.kt.md).
</details>

# /ship 

Running `/ship` is Robert's go-ahead to commit, push and merge the current branch.
Report each step as you go. If any step fails, stop and explain; don't improvise
around it (no force-push, no `--no-verify`, no merging from the command line).

## 1. Pre-flight

- Current branch: `git branch --show-current`. If it's `main`, stop. There's nothing to ship,
  and work should never happen on main.
- Show `git status --short` and `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD`.
- If there are uncommitted changes, check the file list for anything that shouldn't be
  committed (`.env`, credentials, keys, build output, IDE files, large binaries). If
  something looks wrong, stop and ask. Otherwise stage everything and commit with a concise
  message describing the change, ending with the attribution line from the system reminder.
- If there are no commits ahead of `origin/main`, stop. There's nothing to ship.

## 2. Checks

_Placeholder: build, tests, contract validation and the doc-reviewer gate will be
added here later._

## 3. Sync with main

- `git fetch origin`
- If `origin/main` has commits this branch lacks, `git merge origin/main` (a merge, not a
  rebase, so history is preserved). On conflicts, stop and walk Robert through them.

## 4. Push and open the pull request

- `git push -u origin <branch>`
- If a PR for this branch already exists (`gh pr view --json url`), reuse it.
  Otherwise, `gh pr create --base main --head <branch>` with:
  - **Title:** `` if given, otherwise a short summary of the branch's commits.
  - **Body:** a `## Summary` of what changed and why (bullets), a `## Commits` list, and the
    PR attribution line from the system reminder at the end.

## 5. Merge

- `gh pr merge <number> --merge --delete-branch`
  - Always use `--merge`. **Never `--squash` or `--rebase`**, because the assessment reviewers
    want the full commit history. (A PreToolUse hook blocks squash and rebase.)
- `git switch main && git pull --ff-only`
- Delete the local branch if `gh` didn't: `git branch -d <branch>`.

## 6. Report

Give the PR URL, the merge commit SHA, and the commits that were shipped. Remind Robert
that the next piece of work needs a new branch; the branch guard will enforce this.

I also added two interview-prep questions: how you know the race tests would catch an oversell, and why a purchase stays correct with several app instances.

**For the time you have left:** the remaining submission items are:
- the README polish: the "walkthrough pending" note in the purchase row, purchase `curl` examples, and deciding on demo seed data
- checking the README's "Build and run" from a clean clone

You mentioned other plans for after the testing work, so tell me what's next. The next piece of work needs a new branch; the branch guard will stop edits on `main` until then.

I want a way that we can easily see test runs like if i need to go through them during a presentation on the interview. 

I was thinking girhub workflows. What do you think. The tests logs/runs would need to be easy to read the test and read and understand the results.

GitHub Actions is a good fit. It also fills the empty "Checks" step in `/ship` and gives the reviewers a green badge. Here's what I'd build so it's easy to present.

## What you'd show in the interview

1. **Actions tab → the latest run.** The run's summary page is the presentation view. I'd generate a readable report there:
   - **The oversell tests, grouped by what each proves**, just like the README table: *Race tests ✅ 25/25*, *Negative control ✅ 2/2*, *Multi-instance ✅ 6/6*, and so on. You can talk through it top to bottom.
   - **The contract test**, with a line for each endpoint and status.
   - **The load-test numbers**: requests per second, p50/p95/p99 latency, purchases succeeded and refused, and the final stock.
   - **Every test by name.** Your test names are already sentences (`concurrent purchases never sell more than the stock`), so the list reads like a spec.
   - **Failures, if any**, with the assertion message ("oversold: 12 purchases succeeded for a stock of 10"). That's also a great live demo: push a deliberately broken commit, then show it being caught.
2. **The PR page:** a green ✅ "Tests" check on every pull request.
3. **An artifact:** Gradle's full HTML test report, downloadable from the run, for drilling into any test's output.

## How I'd build it

- **Workflow:** `.github/workflows/tests.yml`, using official actions only (`checkout`, `setup-java` for JDK 21, `gradle/actions/setup-gradle` for caching). Testcontainers works out of the box on GitHub's Ubuntu runners because Docker is preinstalled.
- **Report:** a small Python script turns Gradle's JUnit XML into that grouped Markdown summary. I'd write it myself rather than use a third-party report action, because a generic one can only list classes. Ours can say *what each test proves*, which is the story you're presenting. It's also one less outside dependency with write access to your repo.
- **Two jobs:**
  - **Tests:** `./gradlew build`, about 1–2 minutes.
  - **Load test:** `./gradlew loadTest`. It's slower and noisier, so I wouldn't run it on every push.

One thing to know: GitHub's shared runners are small, so the load numbers there will be lower than on your laptop. That's fine to say in the interview: "a correctness check under load, not a benchmark".

# Runs the test suite and the load test on GitHub's servers and writes a readable report to each
# run's summary page (Actions tab -> a run). The report comes from scripts/test_report.py.
name: Tests

on:
  push:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  # Adds a "Run workflow" button on the Actions tab, e.g. for a fresh run during a demo.
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  tests:
    name: Tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: 21
      # Caches Gradle and its dependencies between runs.
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v6

      # Why: `build` = compile + every test except the load test + package. Testcontainers starts
      # Postgres through the runner's preinstalled Docker, exactly as on a laptop.
      - name: Build and test
        run: ./gradlew build

      # Why: `if: always()` so the report is written even when tests fail; that's when it matters most.
      - name: Test report
        if: always()
        run: python3 scripts/test_report.py build/test-results/test >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

      - name: Upload HTML test report
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: test-report
          path: build/reports/tests/test

  # Why: a separate job runs in parallel with `tests`, so the 20-second load run doesn't make the
  # regular check slower. GitHub's shared runners are small: treat the numbers as a smoke test.
  load-test:
    name: Load test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: 21
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v6

      - name: Load test
        run: ./gradlew loadTest

      - name: Load test report
        if: always()
        run: python3 scripts/test_report.py build/test-results/loadTest >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

      - name: Upload HTML load test report
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: load-test-report
          path: build/reports/tests/loadTest

---
name: ship
description: Ship the current branch. Commits any remaining work, pushes to GitHub, opens a pull request, merges it into main with a merge commit (never squash), and returns to an updated main. Use when Robert says to ship, push, or merge the current work.
argument-hint: "[optional: PR title]"
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# /ship $ARGUMENTS

Running `/ship` is Robert's go-ahead to commit, push and merge the current branch.
Report each step as you go. If any step fails, stop and explain; don't improvise
around it (no force-push, no `--no-verify`, no merging from the command line).

## 1. Pre-flight

- Current branch: `git branch --show-current`. If it's `main`, stop. There's nothing to ship,
  and work should never happen on main.
- Show `git status --short` and `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD`.
- If there are uncommitted changes, check the file list for anything that shouldn't be
  committed (`.env`, credentials, keys, build output, IDE files, large binaries). If
  something looks wrong, stop and ask. Otherwise stage everything and commit with a concise
  message describing the change, ending with the attribution line from the system reminder.
- If there are no commits ahead of `origin/main`, stop. There's nothing to ship.

## 2. Checks

_Placeholder: build, tests, contract validation and the doc-reviewer gate will be
added here later._

## 3. Sync with main

- `git fetch origin`
- If `origin/main` has commits this branch lacks, `git merge origin/main` (a merge, not a
  rebase, so history is preserved). On conflicts, stop and walk Robert through them.

## 4. Push and open the pull request

- `git push -u origin <branch>`
- If a PR for this branch already exists (`gh pr view --json url`), reuse it.
  Otherwise, `gh pr create --base main --head <branch>` with:
  - **Title:** `$ARGUMENTS` if given, otherwise a short summary of the branch's commits.
  - **Body:** a `## Summary` of what changed and why (bullets), a `## Commits` list, and the
    PR attribution line from the system reminder at the end.

## 5. Merge

- `gh pr merge <number> --merge --delete-branch`
  - Always use `--merge`. **Never `--squash` or `--rebase`**, because the assessment reviewers
    want the full commit history. (A PreToolUse hook blocks squash and rebase.)
- `git switch main && git pull --ff-only`
- Delete the local branch if `gh` didn't: `git branch -d <branch>`.

## 6. Report

Give the PR URL, the merge commit SHA, and the commits that were shipped. Remind Robert
that the next piece of work needs a new branch; the branch guard will enforce this.

# Nuuly Inventory API

A small inventory-management REST API built for the Nuuly services assessment. It
receives stock by SKU, processes purchases without overselling, and reports current
inventory levels.

The API contract is [src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml](src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml)
(OpenAPI 3.0.3), and the implementation must conform to it exactly. The original brief
is in [docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt](docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt).

150:**Troubleshooting (Windows):** if `gradlew` says `JAVA_HOME is not set` right after installing
154:## Project layout
226:| [scripts/code_guard.py](scripts/code_guard.py) | Makes Claude Code ask me before Claude writes production code under `src/main/`: I write that code, Claude writes tests and coaches. |
## Project layout

```text
build.gradle.kts         The build: plugins, dependencies, Kotlin/Java settings
settings.gradle.kts      Project name (single-module build)
gradlew, gradle/wrapper/ Gradle wrapper; pins the Gradle version, nothing to install
compose.yaml             Local Postgres for bootRun
src/main/
  kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/
    InventoryApplication.kt   Entry point; component scan starts here
    inventory/                The inventory feature: controller, service, repository, models
      error/                  Domain exceptions and the handler that maps them to HTTP errors
  resources/
    application.yml           Spring Boot configuration
    db/migration/             Flyway SQL migrations (V1__..., V2__...)
    openapi/inventory.yaml    The OpenAPI contract (source of truth)
src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/
  inventory/                  Feature tests: repository, service, controller, contract, races,
                              negative control, multi-instance, property-based, load
  support/                    Shared test setup (Testcontainers Postgres, race helper, HTTP client)
.claude/                 Claude Code configuration (hooks, agents, skills) — see below
CLAUDE.md                Project memory and coding standards for Claude Code
docs/
  learning/
    notes/               Study notes: one per source file, explaining it chunk by chunk
    walkthroughs/        Logs of each /walkthrough session
    kotlin-concepts.md   Index of every Kotlin/Spring concept, linked to its notes
  ai-sessions/           Exported transcripts of every AI session on this project
scripts/                 Hook scripts (branch guard, KDoc check, session export)
```

**Package by feature.** Code is grouped by what it does (`inventory/`), not by technical
layer (`controller/`, `service/`, `repository/`). File names still show the layer, so the
controller → service → repository flow is easy to follow. This is a general JVM/Spring
convention, not a Kotlin rule. One Kotlin difference is worth knowing: Kotlin has no
package-private visibility. Its `internal` modifier means "visible within this Gradle
module", so package boundaries are organizational, not enforced by the compiler.

## Learning Kotlin with this project
